lead: Scattering redirects light out of the core instead of absorbing it on the spot. Two linear mechanisms matter: Rayleigh scattering from density and composition fluctuations frozen into the glass, far smaller than the wavelength, and Mie scattering from imperfections about the size of the wavelength. Rayleigh loss falls as 1/λ⁴, so it sets the loss floor near 1550 nm and explains why early 850 nm systems needed short spans. Mie loss is kept small by clean fabrication.

sections.h3: The mechanism: light leaves the core

blocks.text: Glass is a frozen liquid. As the fiber cools on the draw tower, tiny regions lock in with slightly different density and composition from their neighbours, so the refractive index varies on a scale far below the wavelength. Each small index step re-radiates a little of the passing wave in all directions. Most of that light falls outside the acceptance angle and leaves the core; a small part travels backward.

The scattering event is elastic: the scattered light keeps the wavelength of the incident light, and the glass is not heated where it happens. The light is still lost to the link, and it ends up absorbed in the coating or jacket. Both Rayleigh and Mie scattering are called linear because the loss in dB/km does not depend on the power. Power-dependent scattering is a separate effect, covered in stimulated Brillouin and Raman scattering.
For a single-component glass the Rayleigh scattering coefficient is

γR = (8π³/3λ⁴) n⁸ p² βc k TF
γR is the Rayleigh scattering coefficient in m⁻¹ (nepers per metre); λ is the free-space wavelength in m; n is the refractive index; p is the photoelastic coefficient; βc is the isothermal compressibility in m²/N; k = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann’s constant; TF is the fictive temperature in K, at which the glass structure froze.

Over a length L the power falls by the factor e<sup>−γ<sub>R</sub>L</sup>, so the loss in dB is 10 log₁₀(1/e<sup>−γ<sub>R</sub>L</sup>) = 4.343 γ<sub>R</sub>L. The physics behind 1/λ⁴: each fluctuation acts as a tiny dipole whose radiated field grows as 1/λ², so the scattered power grows as 1/λ⁴.

In practice the loss is written α<sub>R</sub> = C/λ⁴ with λ in µm. For germania-doped single-mode fiber C is about 0.8 dB·km⁻¹·µm⁴, which gives 1.53 dB/km at 850 nm, 0.27 dB/km at 1310 nm and 0.14 dB/km at 1550 nm. Double the wavelength and the loss falls 2⁴ = 16 times. Rayleigh loss can be lowered but not removed: a lower fictive temperature (slower cooling, or annealing) and less dopant in the core reduce it, which is how pure-silica-core fibers reach about 0.15 dB/km in total.

Imperfections comparable in size to the wavelength scatter by the Mie process: a rough or wavy core–cladding boundary, small bubbles, unreacted particles in the preform, strain, and fluctuations in core diameter. Mie scattering is strongest in the forward direction, and its wavelength dependence is weaker than Rayleigh’s. A simple model treats it as 1/λ²: a term of 0.05 dB/km at 1 µm drops to 0.021 dB/km at 1.55 µm, a factor of 2.4 against 5.8 for Rayleigh over the same range.

Mie loss is not a property of the glass. Careful preform making, control of the core diameter, a smoother core–cladding interface and a larger index difference keep it below the Rayleigh term in telecom fiber. A large measured Mie term points to a process fault, not to the material.

examples.question: A single-mode fiber has a Rayleigh loss of 0.14 dB/km at 1550 nm. (a) Estimate the Rayleigh loss at 1310 nm. (b) Estimate it at 850 nm. (c) The measured total loss at 850 nm is 2.0 dB/km; how much is left for absorption, Mie scattering and other terms?
steps: Scaling: α<sub>R</sub>(λ) = α<sub>R</sub>(1550) × (1550/λ)⁴, with λ in nm.
(c) Remainder at 850 nm: 2.0 − 1.55 = 0.45 dB/km. Without more data this is an upper bound on the sum of Mie scattering, the UV absorption tail and waveguide imperfections.
examples.answer: 0.27 dB/km at 1310 nm, 1.55 dB/km at 850 nm, and at most 0.45 dB/km left for the other terms at 850 nm.

examples.question: Silica has a fictive temperature of 1400 K, isothermal compressibility 7 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/N, refractive index 1.46 and photoelastic coefficient 0.286. Find the Rayleigh scattering loss in dB/km at 0.85 µm and at 1.55 µm.
steps: Constant part: n⁸ = 1.46⁸ = 20.66, p² = 0.0818, and β<sub>c</sub>kT<sub>F</sub> = 7 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.381 × 10⁻²³ × 1400 = 1.353 × 10⁻³⁰ m³. Their product is 2.286 × 10⁻³⁰ m³.
Over 1 km: γ<sub>R</sub>L = 0.362, transmission e<sup>−0.362</sup> = 0.696, loss 10 log₁₀(1/0.696) = 1.57 dB/km.
At 1.55 µm: γ<sub>R</sub> falls by (1.55/0.85)⁴ = 11.06, to 3.27 × 10⁻⁵ m⁻¹. Over 1 km γ<sub>R</sub>L = 0.0327, and the loss is 4.343 × 0.0327 = 0.142 dB/km.
examples.answer: About 1.57 dB/km at 0.85 µm and 0.14 dB/km at 1.55 µm, the same values that C = 0.8 dB·km⁻¹·µm⁴ gives.

traps: Writing λ⁴ instead of 1/λ⁴. Rayleigh loss falls as the wavelength rises.
Saying scattering loses no power because it is elastic. The wavelength is unchanged, but the redirected light still leaves the link.
Saying Mie scattering dominates an ordinary telecom fiber. Good fiber keeps the Mie term well below Rayleigh.
Leaving γ<sub>R</sub> in m⁻¹ as if it were dB/km. Multiply by 1000 for km⁻¹, then by 4.343 for dB/km.
Calling Rayleigh loss power-dependent. Linear scattering is fixed by the glass; the stimulated kinds appear only at high power.

quiz.q: What is Rayleigh scattering in a silica fiber?
quiz.a: Elastic scattering by density and composition fluctuations frozen into the glass, much smaller than the wavelength, with loss proportional to 1/λ⁴.

quiz.q: Why does Rayleigh loss fall as 1/λ⁴?
quiz.a: Each small fluctuation radiates like a dipole whose field scales as 1/λ²; the scattered power is the square, so it scales as 1/λ⁴.

quiz.q: A fiber has α<sub>R</sub> = 0.20 dB/km at 1550 nm. Estimate α<sub>R</sub> at 1310 nm.
A Mie term is 0.05 dB/km at 1.0 µm and follows 1/λ². Find it at 1.55 µm.
At 850 nm a fiber shows 2.5 dB/km in total and 1.55 dB/km of Rayleigh loss. What can you say about Mie scattering?
quiz.a: Mie plus absorption plus other terms is at most 2.5 − 1.55 = 0.95 dB/km. Measurements at several wavelengths are needed to separate a 1/λ² Mie term from the absorption tails.
The temperature at which the glass structure froze and stopped rearranging as it cooled; a lower value means less frozen disorder and less Rayleigh loss.

quiz.q: Why is 1550 nm the lowest-loss window and not 1700 nm, where Rayleigh loss is even lower?
quiz.a: Rayleigh loss keeps falling, but beyond about 1.6 µm the infrared absorption tail rises steeply (0.32 dB/km at 1.7 µm), so the sum has its minimum near 1.55 µm, about 0.2 dB/km.

beyond: Rayleigh backscatter is what an OTDR reads to find breaks and loss along a cable, and distributed acoustic sensing listens to its phase to turn a fiber into a long microphone. Hollow-core fibers guide light in air, so the glass Rayleigh term nearly vanishes; they have reached losses near 0.1 dB/km in research. Search for “Rayleigh backscatter OTDR”, “fictive temperature annealing” and “hollow-core fiber loss record”.

figure.caption: Rayleigh loss scaled from 0.14 dB/km at 1550 nm: 0.27 dB/km at 1310 nm and 1.55 dB/km at 850 nm, where a measured 2.0 dB/km leaves at most 0.45 dB/km for other terms. The Mie term falls too, but only as 1/λ², and stays small.
